title: Direct proof
objectives: Prove a statement straight from definitions, such as “the sum of two even numbers is even”.

screens.title: Adding even numbers
screens.prose: Four pairs of even numbers. Add each pair and watch the last column fill in.
screens.question: Fill in each sum.

hints.text: Add the two numbers in each row.
For $-6 + 12$, start at $-6$ and move 12 up.
The sums are 6, 18, 6 and 14.

feedback.correct: Right. 6, 18, 6 and 14: every sum is even.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two numbers on each row.

byKey.r2c1: $-6 + 12$ is 6. Start at $-6$ and count 12 up.

explain.text: The sums are 6, 18, 6 and 14. Each one is 2 times a whole number. So far, even plus even has always been even.

screens.title: Is that enough?
screens.prose: Claim: the sum of any two even integers is even. We have four cases, including a negative number and zero.
screens.question: Does checking more cases settle the claim?

options.text: No. There are infinitely many pairs, and checks only ever cover some of them.
Yes. The four pairs include a negative and a zero, so every kind is covered.
options.why: You treated variety as completeness. Infinitely many pairs are still unchecked.

options.text: Yes, once we have checked a million pairs.
options.why: You trusted a large count. A million cases still leave infinitely many untested.

options.text: No, because one of the four sums is odd.
options.why: You misread a sum. 6, 18, 6 and 14 are all even.

hints.text: How many pairs of even integers are there?
Each check covers one pair.
Infinitely many pairs means no list of checks is complete.

feedback.correct: Right. Cases are evidence. A proof has to cover every pair at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether any finite list of checks covers every pair.

byKey.variety: You counted kinds of numbers, not pairs. $2 + 4$ and $4 + 2$ do not settle $1002 + 46$.

explain.text: Every check covers one pair, and there are infinitely many pairs. To cover them all we need letters that stand for any even numbers. That is what a proof does.

screens.title: The proof
screens.prose: A **direct proof** starts from the hypothesis and the definitions. It reaches the conclusion one justified step at a time. Even means $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: $j + k$ is an integer, so $a + b$ is even. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: You kept an example. It covers one pair, and the proof must cover every pair.

hints.text: Start by naming the two numbers.
Next, write each one with the definition of even.
Let; $a = 2j$; $b = 2k$; $a + b = 2(j + k)$; so even.

feedback.correct: Right. Name the numbers, unpack the definition, add, and repack.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Introduce $a$ and $b$, unpack each, then add.

byKey.d1: You kept the example. A proof uses letters so that one argument covers every pair.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.
byKey.s4: The sum can only be written once $a$ and $b$ are unpacked.

explain.text: We named two arbitrary even integers and wrote each as 2 times an integer. Adding gave 2 times $j + k$. Since $j + k$ is an integer, the sum fits the definition of even.

screens.title: Why is $j + k$ an integer?
screens.prose: The last line says $j + k$ is an integer. A stranger checking the proof will ask why.
screens.question: Which reason justifies that line?

options.text: The sum of two integers is an integer.
$j$ and $k$ are even.
options.why: You assumed $j$ and $k$ are even. They are any integers: $6 = 2 \times 3$.

options.text: Because $a + b$ is even.
options.why: You used the conclusion to justify a step. That is circular.

options.text: It holds for $j = 1$ and $k = 2$.
options.why: You checked one example. The line must hold for every $j$ and $k$.

hints.text: What do we know about $j$ and $k$?
They are integers, nothing more.
Adding two integers always gives an integer.

feedback.correct: Right. Integers are closed under addition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use only what the proof knows about $j$ and $k$.

byKey.circ: You justified the step with the claim itself. The proof must reach $a + b$ even, not assume it.

explain.text: All we know is that $j$ and $k$ are integers. The sum of two integers is an integer. So $2(j + k)$ has the form $2 \times \text{integer}$.

screens.title: Odd plus odd
screens.prose: Odd means $n = 2k + 1$ for some integer $k$. Claim: odd plus odd is even. Let $a = 2j + 1$ and $b = 2k + 1$.
screens.question: $a + b = 2(\ \square\ )$. What goes in the bracket?

hints.text: Add the two expressions.
Take out the factor 2: $2(j + k + 1)$.

feedback.correct: Right. $a + b = 2j + 2k + 2 = 2(j + k + 1)$, and $j + k + 1$ is an integer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add first, then take out the factor 2.

byKey.noone: You dropped the two 1s. $1 + 1 = 2$ gives the extra 1 inside the bracket.
byKey.two: You took out the 2 from $2j$ and $2k$ but not from the final 2.

explain.text: $(2j + 1) + (2k + 1) = 2j + 2k + 2$. Each term has a factor 2, so the sum is $2(j + k + 1)$. That is 2 times an integer, so it is even.

screens.title: Odd times odd
screens.prose: Claim: odd times odd is odd. The rectangle has sides $2j + 1$ and $2k + 1$. Its four pieces add to $4jk + 2j + 2k + 1$.
screens.question: $(2j + 1)(2k + 1) = 2(\ \square\ ) + 1$. What goes in the bracket?

hints.text: Three of the pieces have a factor 2.
$4jk + 2j + 2k = 2(\ldots)$.
Halve each of $4jk$, $2j$ and $2k$: $2jk + j + k$.

feedback.correct: Right. $(2j + 1)(2k + 1) = 2(2jk + j + k) + 1$, which is odd.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the factor 2 out of the three big pieces only.

byKey.nohalf: You left the three pieces as they are. Inside the bracket each one is halved.
byKey.keep1: You moved the 1 inside the bracket. It stays outside: that is the odd part.

explain.text: The three big pieces each have a factor 2, so together they are $2(2jk + j + k)$. The corner piece is the 1 left over. So the product is 2 times an integer, plus 1: odd.

screens.title: One letter, two numbers
screens.prose: A classmate hands in this proof that even plus even is even. Each line after line 2 follows from the one before.
screens.question: Tap the line that breaks the proof.

hints.text: Check what each line allows $a$ and $b$ to be.
Line 2 uses the letter $k$ twice.
With one $k$, $a = b$. The proof covers $4 + 4$ but not $2 + 4$.

feedback.correct: Right. One $k$ for both numbers forces $a = b$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the line that quietly makes the two numbers equal.

byKey.r0: Line 1 sets up the claim correctly. Look at how the next line picks its letters.
byKey.r2: Line 3 is right, given line 2. The fault comes earlier.
byKey.r3: Line 4 is right: $4k = 2(2k)$. The fault comes earlier.
byKey.r4: Line 5 follows from line 4. The fault is in how $a$ and $b$ were written.

explain.text: Line 2 uses one $k$ for both numbers, so it proves the claim only when $a = b$. A pair such as $2 + 4$ is never covered. Two numbers need two letters: $a = 2j$ and $b = 2k$.

screens.title: Proof by cases
screens.prose: Claim: $n^2 + n$ is even for every integer $n$. No single formula covers every $n$, so we split into cases that cover them all.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Every integer $n$ is even or odd. We take each case in turn.
Case 1: $n = 2k$. Then $n^2 + n = 4k^2 + 2k$ $= 2(2k^2 + k)$, which is even.
Case 2: $n = 2k + 1$. Then $n^2 + n = (2k + 1)(2k + 2)$ $= 2(2k + 1)(k + 1)$, which is even.
Both cases give an even number, so $n^2 + n$ is even for every integer $n$. $\blacksquare$
Case 2: $n = 3$. Then $n^2 + n = 12$, which is even.
lines.why: You checked one odd number. The case must cover every odd $n$, written $2k + 1$.

hints.text: Say first why two cases are enough.
One case for even $n$, one for odd $n$.
Split; even case; odd case; conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. Two cases that cover every integer, each proved with a letter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split, prove each case for every $n$ of its kind, then conclude.

byKey.d1: You kept the case $n = 3$. It is one example, so odd numbers such as 5 are not covered.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line. Both cases are needed, and so is the line saying they cover every integer.

explain.text: Every integer is even or odd, so the two cases cover everything. Each case uses a letter, so it covers every number of its kind. Leaving out either case would leave half the integers unproved.

screens.title: Direct proof
screens.prose:
To prove *if $P$ then $Q$* directly, assume $P$ and write out the definitions. Then reach $Q$ one justified step at a time:

$$P \;\Rightarrow\; \text{definitions} \;\Rightarrow\; \cdots \;\Rightarrow\; Q$$

The letters must cover every case the claim covers.
screens.question: Which numbers does the even-plus-even proof cover?

options.text: Every even integer, including $0$ and $-6$
Positive even numbers only
options.why: You assumed even numbers are positive. $0 = 2 \times 0$ and $-6 = 2 \times (-3)$ both fit $2k$.

options.text: Every even number except 0
options.why: You left out 0. It is even, since $0 = 2 \times 0$.

options.text: Every integer, even or odd
options.why: You dropped the hypothesis. The proof writes $a = 2j$, and $3 + 4 = 7$ is odd.

feedback.correct: Right. $k$ may be any integer, so 0 and negative even numbers are covered.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which numbers can be written $2k$ with $k$ an integer.

explain.text: $k$ ranges over every integer, positive, zero or negative. So $0 = 2 \times 0$ and $-6 = 2 \times (-3)$ are even. The proof never assumed the numbers were positive, so it covers them too.

screens.title: Two kinds of average
screens.prose: For $a, b \ge 0$, the **arithmetic mean** is $\tfrac{a + b}{2}$ and the **geometric mean** is $\sqrt{ab}$. Claim: $\tfrac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$. A direct proof starts from a fact we already trust.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $a, b \ge 0$. A square is never negative, so $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0$.
Squaring the claim gives $\tfrac{(a + b)^2}{4} \ge ab$, which is true, so the claim holds.
lines.why: You started from the claim. A chain from the claim to something true proves nothing on its own.

hints.text: Start from a square, which is never negative.
Expand $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2$.
Square; expand; add $2\sqrt{ab}$; divide by 2.

feedback.correct: Right. From a true starting fact, forwards to the claim.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the square that is at least 0, then rearrange.

byKey.d1: You kept the line that starts from the claim. A proof must run from known facts to the claim.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line. Each rearranging step is needed.

explain.text: $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$ and $\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$ need $a, b \ge 0$. Expanding the square gives $a - 2\sqrt{ab} + b \ge 0$. Rearranging gives the claim, with equality only when $a = b$.

screens.title: Average return and real growth
screens.prose: A fund returns $+50\%$ one year and $-50\%$ the next. The growth factors are 1.5 and 0.5, with arithmetic mean 1.0. The geometric mean is the steady factor that gives the same two-year growth.
screens.question: What is the geometric mean $\sqrt{1.5 \times 0.5}$, to 4 decimal places?

hints.text: Multiply the two factors first.

feedback.correct: Right. $\sqrt{0.75} \approx 0.8660$, below the arithmetic mean of 1.0, as the proof says.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 1.5 by 0.5, then take the square root.

byKey.am: You gave the arithmetic mean. The geometric mean is $\sqrt{1.5 \times 0.5}$.
byKey.prod: You stopped at the product. Take its square root.

explain.text: £100 becomes £150, then £75, so two years at 0.8660 each match the fund. An average return of 0% lost a quarter of the money. That gap between the two means is volatility drag.

ideas: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and writes out the definitions. It reaches the conclusion one justified step at a time.
Even means $n = 2k$ and odd means $n = 2k + 1$, for some integer $k$. Two numbers need two letters.
Examples are evidence. A proof by cases is fine when the cases cover every possibility.

formula.name: Even plus even
formula.note: $j + k$ is an integer, so the sum is even.

summary.trap: Writing $a = 2k$ and $b = 2k$ with one letter proves the claim only when $a = b$.

quiz.prose: $a \mid b$ means $b = am$ for some integer $m$. Claim: if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$ then $a \mid c$. We have $b = am$ and $c = bn$ for integers $m$, $n$.
quiz.question: Which line finishes the proof?

options.text: $c = (am)n = a(mn)$, and $mn$ is an integer, so $a \mid c$.
$c = am + n$, so $a \mid c$.
options.why: You added the multipliers. Substituting $b = am$ into $c = bn$ multiplies them.

options.text: $3 \mid 6$ and $6 \mid 24$, and $3 \mid 24$.
options.why: You gave one example. The claim is about every $a$, $b$ and $c$.

options.text: $c = a(mn)$, so $a \mid c$.
options.why: You skipped the reason. The definition needs $mn$ to be an integer, so say so.

feedback.correct: Right. Substitute, regroup, and say why $mn$ is an integer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $b = am$ into $c = bn$.

explain.text: Substituting gives $c = (am)n = a(mn)$. The product of two integers is an integer. So $c$ is $a$ times an integer, which is the definition of $a \mid c$.

quiz.prose: A student writes: "$2 + 4 = 6$ and $8 + 10 = 18$, so the sum of two even numbers is always even."
quiz.question: What is wrong with it?

options.text: It checks two cases, and the claim is about infinitely many pairs.
The claim is false.
options.why: The claim is true. The trouble is the argument, not the claim.

options.text: It needs at least ten examples.
options.why: You asked for more examples. No number of examples covers every pair.

options.text: Nothing: both sums are even.
options.why: Both sums are even, but two cases cannot settle every case.

feedback.correct: Right. Examples are evidence, not a proof.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether two cases cover every pair.

explain.text: Two examples cover two pairs out of infinitely many. A proof uses letters, $a = 2j$ and $b = 2k$, to cover them all. The claim is true, but this is not a proof of it.

quiz.prose: A proof that $n^2 + n$ is even handles only the case $n = 2k$.
quiz.question: Why is the case $n = 2k + 1$ needed as well?

options.text: Odd integers are not of the form $2k$, so without it they are unproved.
The odd case is harder, so it is the one that counts.
options.why: You ranked the cases. Each case covers different numbers, and both are needed.

options.text: To check the even case was right.
options.why: The odd case checks nothing about the even case. It covers other numbers.

options.text: It is not needed: one case is enough.
options.why: You stopped at one case. 3, 5 and 7 are not of the form $2k$.

feedback.correct: Right. The cases must cover every integer between them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which integers the first case leaves out.

explain.text: The form $2k$ covers only even integers. The odd ones need $2k + 1$. Only the two cases together cover every integer.

quiz.prose: A fund returns $+20\%$ one year and $-20\%$ the next, starting from £100.
quiz.question: What is it worth after the two years, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply 1.2, then 0.8, to £100.

byKey.flat: You added the returns, $+20\% - 20\% = 0$. Returns multiply: $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$.
byKey.back: You stopped after the first year.

explain.text: $100 \times 1.2 = 120$ and $120 \times 0.8 = 96$. The arithmetic mean of 1.2 and 0.8 is 1.0, but the geometric mean is $\sqrt{0.96} \approx 0.9798$. The fund lost £4.
